blocks.p: EMDR is a very popular treatment option for pretty much everything at this point, though it began as a treatment for trauma. You're probably seeing it everywhere, and there's a good chance you've worked with a therapist who uses EMDR.

When most people think of EMDR, they picture a therapist waving a finger in front of someone's face, and that's it. That image has become shorthand, and the shorthand causes a lot of confusion when it comes to accurately assessing what's actually helpful about EMDR. So let's look at what EMDR is beyond the eye movements, whether EMDR is helpful based on research, and, even more interesting, what research says about what's helpful about EMDR.

For context: I'm a therapist licensed in California, and I've been practicing for about 17 years with a wide range of populations. I primarily use a blend of very present-moment-focused, body-based, and solution-oriented techniques.
The first thing is to understand what EMDR actually is. This changes how you hear everything that comes after. To do that, let's look briefly at the eight-phase structure of EMDR.
Phase one is history taking and treatment planning. The therapist gathers context, identifies target memories, and judges whether the person is ready to begin trauma processing.

Phase two is preparation and stabilization. The therapist explains the EMDR process, builds rapport, and teaches the client grounding skills and ways to manage when things get intense, which they very likely will, just due to the nature of talking about traumatic incidents.

Phase three is assessment. Here the therapist and the client activate a specific memory and identify its components: the image, the negative belief attached to it, the positive belief the client wants instead, the emotions, the bodily sensations. They measure the distress and the believability of the new belief, setting baselines before processing starts.

Phase four is desensitization. This is the one almost everyone thinks of when they hear EMDR. In this phase, the client holds the target memory in mind while following bilateral stimulation of some sort, and the therapist continues the bilateral stimulation until the distress reduces.
Phase five is installation, where the therapist again uses bilateral stimulation to strengthen a new, adaptive belief.
Phase six is the body scan. The client holds the memory and the new adaptive belief, and then scans the body for any residual tension. If tension shows up, additional processing can follow.
Phase seven is closure. Sessions end with containment strategies and a return to baseline, so the client leaves feeling stable whether or not the processing was completed.
And finally, phase eight is reevaluation. At the next session, the therapist checks whether the gains have held, whether the target is still processed, and whether new targets need attention.

Notice where bilateral stimulation shows up. It's mainly in phases four and five, and, if needed, six. That means the eye movements, or taps, or sounds, or whatever, are a part of the process, but they're not the whole therapy.

Viewed as a cohesive whole, the vast majority of EMDR is not very special. Once you remove the bilateral stimulation component, it involves assessment and treatment planning, rapport building, managing distress, questioning beliefs and thought replacement, bodily awareness, discussing past traumatic incidents, and reevaluating and making new goals. All of these are fairly typical therapy components. If you ask any therapist whether they do any of these pieces, they'll probably say yes, and that they do many of them in some combination. Likely all of them.

The short, evidence-based answer is yes. Multiple organizations have recognized EMDR as an effective treatment for PTSD. The American Psychological Association includes it among evidence-based options. Well, sort of; there's a caveat. They list it as a second-tier option. The APA says it's more helpful than being on a wait list and more helpful than treatment as usual, and that the pros of EMDR outweigh the cons. So it's better than standing around doing nothing, and probably better than very basic talk therapy. That's something.
The World Health Organization lists EMDR as a standard, and the United States Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense give EMDR a strong recommendation.

In randomized trials, EMDR consistently outperforms wait-list controls and nonspecific treatments. That's important, but it doesn't tell us much beyond the fact that the protocol does more than the passage of time or simple attention. People get better, and evidence shows that EMDR helps them get better. That's important.

But that's only half the question. When researchers compare EMDR to other trauma-focused therapies, like cognitive processing therapy, trauma-focused CBT, or prolonged exposure, the outcomes are, broadly speaking, similar. Direct comparisons tend to show equivalent reductions in PTSD symptoms. That pattern shows up across multiple trials and meta-analyses.
So what does that tell us? It suggests EMDR is an effective path to healing, but not necessarily a unique one. Different roads can lead to the same place.

So let's talk about what those shared roads look like. In psychotherapy research, common factors emerge: elements that appear across different therapies and explain much of why they work. For trauma therapies, these common factors are maybe especially relevant. I'll give you four.

The first is the therapeutic alliance. The relationship between therapist and client is a major predictor of positive outcomes across almost every form of therapy. I would say every form of therapy, actually. That bond, the therapist's empathy, the attunement, the ability to repair ruptures: these create predictability and a safe other to heal with. This co-regulation process, from therapist to client, creates a platform for safety. It will even activate the body's ventral vagal pathways, which are responsible for many cognitive, social, and health benefits when active. And when they're active, the therapy techniques become useful. So when you're in safety, techniques become useful, whether that's challenging false beliefs or telling the trauma narrative.

The second is exposure. Processing a traumatic memory by holding it in mind while staying present is exposure. In EMDR, the client activates the memory and stays with it during desensitization. In prolonged exposure, the person repeatedly recounts the narrative. Trauma-focused CBT has the client tell the narrative repeatedly as well. The formats differ, but all of these involve confronting the memory rather than avoiding it. Exposure allows the brain and the body to relearn that the memory is a memory and not a current threat.

The recovery part of exposure is also important; I would say extremely important. The system learns that it can access discomfort, whether through a memory or something else, and then recover from it. Doing so repeatedly builds the body's distress tolerance.

The third is expectancy and hope. Belief that the therapy will work matters. Positive expectation is mobilizing. Somebody with hope is more likely to take action and make the most of their therapy time, no matter what style the therapist is using. Simply having hope is big, and having hope with a safe other is even bigger.

The fourth is cognitive reprocessing. Most therapies involve some level of questioning thoughts, whether through reframing them, reality testing, or something else. Many of my clients will explicitly ask me to call them out on their thinking, like when they're avoiding things by making excuses, or rationalizing or minimizing their pain. People want clearer thinking. They want to be called out on it.
These elements, and more, show up across various therapies. They are not unique to EMDR. They account for a large share of positive outcomes regardless of the modality a therapist uses.

So we've addressed whether EMDR is effective. But there's a much more interesting question: do the eye movements, or other forms of bilateral stimulation, matter? Are they the active ingredient that makes EMDR special, or just an accessory on top of the things that actually work?

People have tried to answer this question with dismantling studies. These are clinical trials that compare full EMDR with versions that remove the bilateral stimulation or put other controls in its place. Research trials comparing EMDR with and without eye movements found no significant difference in PTSD symptoms. A meta-analysis of several dismantling studies found no statistically significant advantage for bilateral stimulation. Another meta-analysis found a moderate benefit to eye movements in lab-based studies, but this benefit was inconsistent in clinical PTSD trials. So a benefit in the lab, but not so much outside the lab.

You might be wondering why lab results would be different from clinical trials. There are many potential reasons. In lab studies, everyone is on their best behavior. They're following protocols. They know they're being monitored, maybe evaluated, and so they provide the best possible treatment they can. In controlled trials, therapists are also more likely to be trained for the study and supervised, unlike the real clinical world, where therapists act more in silos.

On top of that, the client may be experiencing a next-level placebo, where they subconsciously buy into the process even more due to the nature of the lab experiment, the professionals, the data, and so on. Another reason is that lab participants often have less intense PTSD symptoms, or they're asked to focus on distressing memories but not necessarily traumatic ones. And these participants are often student volunteers.

There are also critiques of how the EMDR field has responded to these findings. When early dismantling studies failed to find a difference, EMDR training materials and manuals were updated to emphasize different dosages and variants of bilateral stimulation. When different modes of bilateral stimulation, like tapping, showed similar outcomes, tapping became framed as a legitimate variant of EMDR rather than a distinct control that proves otherwise.

Obviously, if the unique feature of EMDR can be expanded to include other things, then it's not unique. I once talked to a fellow therapist who had just returned from an EMDR conference, and they were convinced that walking was now an EMDR intervention. Walking. Why? Because it involves alternating bilateral movement. And you're right: that sounds odd. At some point, if everything counts, tapping or sounds or walking, then really nothing is being tested. Critics rightfully argue that this looks like moving the goalposts, and I'd say that's a very serious critique.

The field of psychology advances by testing hypotheses with a willingness to accept inconvenient answers. If the specific mechanism you name as central to your modality fails repeated tests, the honest response is to revise the theory, rather than to redefine the terms so your treatment still fits the original claim. That is fairly questionable, if not shady, in my opinion. If you do a deeper dive into EMDR and its founder, Shapiro, there's more questionableness to it. I highly recommend the YouTube video from Neural Transmissions titled "A Hard Look at EMDR and Its Unscrupulous Founder."
As I said, EMDR is supported by evidence, but the evidence has weaknesses.

One major concern is allegiance bias. Many EMDR studies are conducted by clinicians who train in and promote EMDR. Across psychotherapy research, studies run by invested parties tend to produce larger effect sizes, basically more benefit. That doesn't automatically invalidate things, but it does mean we need more independent replications.

Also, sample sizes in many trials have been small, which weakens statistical power and increases uncertainty. And publication bias is always a concern. Negative or null trials are less likely to be published, which inflates what we think is true about EMDR.
These shortcomings, by the way, are not just an EMDR issue. Psychotherapy studies in large part have major problems like these.
Let's do a little thought experiment to illustrate the overall point.

Imagine you were coming to me for therapy because I have a revolutionary new method that has shown great results. I help my clients process their trauma by telling the trauma narrative, the story, but while they do so, they flex and curl their toes and then release them. It's called Toe Curling Desensitization and Reprocessing, or TCDR.

At first you think, "Justin, you want me to tell you my traumas, the most horrific things in my life, while curling my toes?" It seems weird to you. I assure you that toe curling creates a rhythmic motor pattern that occupies a portion of working memory and thereby reduces the vividness of the traumatic image while you hold it in mind.

TCDR still sounds silly to you, but the reasoning I give you sounds fancy enough, and you can't argue with the studies that say there's benefit. And everyone's talking about it, and Bessel van der Kolk raves about it in The Body Keeps the Score, a book you love. So you cautiously agree to meet with me, desperate for change.

When we meet, I don't just ask you to clench and release your toes, obviously. I greet you at the door and invite you in. The office is calming, with natural greens and blues. It's quiet, and there's a nice view out the window overlooking the water. We smile together and chitchat a bit. We talk about the weather. I learn more about you and assess your needs. We make a treatment plan together. Basic therapy stuff.

Then, as you're ready, you tell me your traumatic life context. Yes, while curling and releasing your toes. It's not pleasant to talk about this stuff, but you're okay. You recover. We process what happened. You get homework, and we meet again the following week.

I suspect TCDR would be just as effective as EMDR. Not because of the toe curling, which is obviously not necessary, even though it might sound plausible, but because of the common factors of therapy. The toe curling is dressing. It's cosmetic, and ultimately unnecessary.
So what's the practical takeaway?
First, EMDR is an evidence-based option. If you've found a clinician who uses EMDR, and you feel safe and supported and you're making progress, that is meaningful and positive, and I'm happy for you.

Second, many of the helpful components of EMDR are not unique to EMDR. Actually, the majority of it. Safety building, co-regulation, gradual exposure, cognitive change, and more show up in effective therapies across the board. You do not need EMDR to get those ingredients.

Third, the central signature of EMDR, bilateral stimulation, especially with the eyes, is probably not essential for the bulk of its clinical effects. The research suggests it may add a small effect in tightly controlled lab conditions, but in the messy reality of therapy, it is not the engine driving recovery.

That conclusion should be more liberating than upsetting, especially for potential clients. Healing trauma is not locked behind a single ritual or a single technique. If you're worried you missed something because you didn't have EMDR, or you're choosing between therapists and the only option is someone who practices prolonged exposure or cognitive processing therapy, or something else, that's okay.

Focus instead on the practical markers of good care: a therapist who prioritizes safety, who can help you regulate, who builds a steady alliance, who introduces the work slowly, and who helps you make meaning of change. Those pieces are essential.

As a therapist and coach, I also use gradual exposure to discomfort. But instead of asking clients to tell me trauma narratives, we focus on emotions that are typically difficult to acknowledge, difficult to pay attention to, difficult to feel. They're there anyway, so we have to pay attention to them.

We pay attention within, or slightly past, the edge of what the client can tolerate, and then we recover. Once back at a baseline, we can try again, if they'd like and if they're ready. Over time, typically within a single session, these emotions become much more tolerable. Not cured, I'm not saying that, but much more tolerable. And then we can target more difficult ones as their capacity allows.
Personally, I don't think there's a need to add anything else to the mix, like eye movements, or tapping, or sounds. Not even clenched toes. You can if you want.

To wrap up: EMDR gives clinicians and clients a structured path toward change. Bilateral stimulation is part of that path, but probably not the sole reason the path exists, and probably not even a necessary piece of it.

That puts power back into your hands as a potential therapy client. You have lots of choices. Healing is not a trick. It's not a gimmick. It's not a hack. It's a reliable set of practices built on top of safety, and on all those wonderful co-regulation pieces of therapy that all styles should have in common.
